oil.summary: A sharp WTI/Brent divergence dominated oil markets Thursday. WTI tumbled 3.70% to $98.02/bbl while Brent edged up 1.17% to $110.06/bbl, a spread that reflects the competing forces of Trump's Russian sanctions waivers — which have rerouted Arctic-grade barrels to Asian buyers via the Northern Sea Route — against ongoing Hormuz/Bab al-Mandab disruptions that tighten Atlantic Basin supply. Three tankers damaged in the Gulf this week, fresh Houthi strikes on Saudi energy sites, and Ukraine's 1,015-drone assault on Russian oil facilities kept the geopolitical premium elevated for Brent. Refined products cracked hard: Heating Oil collapsed 6.15% to $4.6221/gal and RBOB fell 1.69% to $3.0645/gal. US crude stocks drew down 3.1 million barrels per the latest EIA print. CME OPEC Watch prices a 77% probability of a production cut at the next meeting.
drivers: WTI/Brent spread blowing out as Trump's Russia sanction waivers redirect discounted barrels east, softening WTI while Brent holds on Gulf/Hormuz risk premium
Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab disruptions — three tankers damaged, ongoing Houthi strikes on Saudi sites — supporting Atlantic Basin crude but crushing refined product flows
Bearish US refinery margin signal: Heating Oil -6.15% and RBOB -1.69% despite a 3.1 mb crude stock draw, suggesting demand destruction at high retail prices

gas.summary: Henry Hub and TTF are moving in opposite directions, highlighting a deepening transatlantic gas market split. Henry Hub slid 6.28% to $2.777/MMBtu on the day, extending a brutal 13.16% weekly decline, likely reflecting mild weather and comfortable domestic supply. TTF gained 2.87% to €87.5/MWh, up 19.31% on the month, as the EU formally rejected any US-brokered restoration of Russian gas imports under a prospective Ukraine peace deal, keeping European supply constraints intact. The UK government's re-approval of the Jackdaw North Sea gas field offers some medium-term supply relief but does nothing for near-term TTF tightness. North Sea asset turnover accelerated as BP continues its full exit from UK upstream and independents step in.
drivers: EU's outright rejection of resumed Russian gas imports under a peace framework cements TTF's structurally elevated level, now +19% on the month
Henry Hub in freefall (-13% on the week) on soft US demand fundamentals, widening the TTF/HH arb and incentivising continued LNG export flows to Europe
UK Jackdaw field re-approval adds long-term North Sea supply optionality, but BP's full upstream exit signals major incumbents are de-risking UK gas exposure

power.summary: Power and carbon data are thin today. EU Carbon EUAs edged fractionally lower, down 0.21% to $81.47/EUA, continuing a modest weekly and monthly retreat of 2.61% and 1.18% respectively, despite TTF natural gas rising 2.87% on the day — a divergence that would normally pressure carbon higher via gas-to-coal switching economics. The disconnect may reflect broader risk-off sentiment given escalating conflict headlines. Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv's energy infrastructure, reported Monday, remain the most acute power-sector risk in theatre. On the corporate side, oil supermajors are flagging record quarterly profits tied to the Middle East war premium, though capex discipline is being maintained. Beyond these points, today's provided data for this sector is limited.
drivers: EUA prices drifting lower (-2.6% on the week) despite surging gas costs, suggesting near-term demand-side weakness is outweighing fuel-switching carbon pressure
Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure represent a direct power-grid threat and could amplify winter supply stress across Eastern Europe
Supermajors banking war-premium profits while capping spending, signalling no imminent upstream capacity relief that could ease power generation fuel costs
